fun_facts: Blacktip sharks feed by ambushing schools of baitfish from below at speed, and the momentum often carries them clean out of the water in a spinning leap, a signature move so similar to the aptly named spinner shark that anglers, and even some biologists, struggle to tell the two apart at a glance.

Outside the spring mating season, male and female blacktip sharks mostly keep to separate schools, sometimes even using different stretches of the same coastline, so a tagger working one group of adults is often tagging one sex at a time without realizing it.

A blacktip shark matures late for an animal that tops out around six feet: males at 4 to 5 years old, females not until 6 or 7, a slow start that is part of why an overfished blacktip population takes so long to rebuild.

measures.label: Fork length
measures.help: Tip of the snout to the fork of the tail, measured in a straight line.

vocabs.label: Sex
vocabs.help: Males have a pair of claspers on the inner pelvic fins; females do not.

vocabs.label: Condition at release
vocabs.help: Sharks are unusually sensitive to capture stress; how it left the gear matters as much as its size.

not_taggable.reason: a shark in poor condition or bleeding is unlikely to survive release, so tagging it wastes the tag and the reward

must_release.reason: under the federal Atlantic HMS recreational minimum size for this shark grouping, 54 inches fork length
